items.question: The 73rd Constitutional Amendment created local governments, but genuine self-government still eludes the panchayats. Examine the reasons, with reference to the devolution of the '3 Fs'.
items.modelAnswer:
The **73rd Amendment (1992)** gave panchayats constitutional status through **Part IX (Arts 243–243O)** and the **Eleventh Schedule (29 subjects)**, mandating a three-tier structure, reserved seats (one-third for women), a five-year term, a **State Election Commission (243K)** and a **State Finance Commission (243I)**. It thus deepened democracy to the grassroots and created a genuine third tier of the federal polity.

However, real empowerment has lagged because effective decentralisation depends on transferring the **'3 Fs' — funds, functions and functionaries** — and the Constitution left this to the **discretion of State Legislatures (Art 243G)**. The consequences are visible: (i) **functions** — most states devolve only a few of the 29 subjects, with parallel line departments and parastatals retaining control of health, education and water; (ii) **funds** — panchayats have thin own-revenues, cannot tax without state sanction (243H), and **State Finance Commission** recommendations are only advisory; (iii) **functionaries** — panchayats lack dedicated staff and technical support, and deputed officials often dominate elected representatives. Political interference by MLAs/MPs, proxy representation ('Sarpanch-Pati'), and weak accountability further dilute autonomy.

Remedies flow from the **2nd ARC's report on local governance**: adopt **'activity mapping'** to fix each tier's role, guarantee untied funds, create a separate panchayat cadre (as in Karnataka), strengthen Gram Sabhas for bottom-up planning, and make State Finance Commission compliance enforceable. **Kerala and Karnataka** show that where the 3 Fs are genuinely devolved, PRIs become effective. **Andhra Pradesh's Grama/Ward Sachivalayam-cum-Volunteer model (2019)** shows a parallel push for doorstep delivery, though it must reinforce — not bypass — elected panchayats. Real self-government, therefore, requires converting a permissive constitutional scheme into mandatory, funded devolution.
keyPoints: 73rd Amendment: Part IX, 29-subject Eleventh Schedule, SEC (243K), SFC (243I), reservations, 5-year term.
Core gap: devolution of the 3 Fs (funds, functions, functionaries) is discretionary under Art 243G.
Functions poorly devolved; funds thin and SFC advice non-binding; functionaries lacking / deputed staff dominate.
Political interference, proxy representation and weak accountability further erode autonomy.
2nd ARC remedies: activity mapping, untied funds, separate cadre (Karnataka), stronger Gram Sabhas.
AP angle: Grama/Ward Sachivalayam (2019) aids doorstep delivery but should reinforce elected panchayats.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Indian Polity: Local Self-Government (issues; 2nd ARC); Andhra Pradesh Grama/Ward Sachivalayam programme (2019)

items.question: Discuss the objectives and significance of the PESA Act, 1996 in extending self-governance to tribal areas. How is it relevant to Andhra Pradesh?
items.modelAnswer:
Since **Part IX does not automatically apply to the Fifth Schedule areas (Article 243M)**, Parliament used its power to extend it with modifications through the **Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 (PESA)**. Its objective is to extend panchayats to Scheduled areas while adapting them to **tribal self-rule and customary practice**, rather than imposing a uniform model.

PESA's significance lies in making the **Gram Sabha the pivot** of governance in tribal areas: it must approve village development plans and beneficiary lists, exercise control over **minor forest produce, minor water bodies and land**, be consulted before land acquisition and resettlement, safeguard **community resources and customs**, and check the transfer of tribal land. It also bars higher-tier panchayats from encroaching on the powers of lower tiers. In effect PESA converts formal decentralisation into **substantive tribal empowerment** and is a bulwark against alienation of tribal land and resources.

For **Andhra Pradesh** the Act is directly relevant because the state has **Fifth Schedule Scheduled areas** in its agency/tribal tracts (e.g., the erstwhile Visakhapatnam and East Godavari agency regions). Here PESA-empowered Gram Sabhas, read with laws restricting non-tribal land transfer, are meant to protect Adivasi communities. Yet implementation gaps — dilution of Gram Sabha consent, mining and displacement pressures, and weak devolution of the 3 Fs — limit its promise. Strengthening Gram Sabha capacity, honouring free prior consent, and firmly enforcing PESA rules are essential so that constitutional protection for Scheduled areas becomes a lived reality in Andhra Pradesh.
keyPoints: Part IX does not apply to Fifth Schedule areas (243M); PESA, 1996 extends it with tribal modifications.
Objectives: participatory village governance aligned with tribal customs and traditions.
Makes Gram Sabha central — control over minor forest produce, water, land, consent on acquisition.
Bars higher tiers from encroaching on lower-tier powers; protects tribal land and resources.
AP relevance: state has Fifth Schedule agency areas where PESA + land-transfer laws protect Adivasis.
Challenges: diluted Gram Sabha consent, mining/displacement, weak devolution — needs firm enforcement.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Indian Polity: Local Self-Government (PESA Act; Scheduled areas)

items.question: Andhra Pradesh's Grama/Ward Sachivalayam and Volunteer system is described as a model of last-mile governance. Evaluate its design, benefits and limitations.
items.modelAnswer:
Launched on **2 October 2019**, Andhra Pradesh's **Grama/Ward Sachivalayam (Village/Ward Secretariat)** system created a permanent administrative layer for **doorstep delivery of government services**. About **15,004 Grama Sachivalayams** in rural areas and **3,842 Ward Sachivalayams** in urban areas were set up, each staffed by a cluster of dedicated functionaries and supported by **Grama/Ward Volunteers**, each looking after roughly **50 households**.

Its design merits are notable: a **single-window** secretariat brings hundreds of services (certificates, pensions, welfare enrolment) close to citizens; **Volunteers** enable **last-mile, transparent delivery** of Direct Benefit Transfer schemes, reducing intermediaries and leakages; and large-scale recruitment addressed the chronic **functionary deficit** that hampers local governance elsewhere. It complements the constitutional framework by giving the administration real presence at the village/ward level.

The model also has limitations. As an **executive/administrative structure**, it must not **overshadow the elected Gram Panchayat and Gram Sabha**, whose primacy the 73rd Amendment guarantees; concentrating delivery in state-appointed staff and Volunteers risks weakening elected self-government and inviting political capture. Sustaining a very large workforce raises **fiscal** questions, and Volunteers handling citizen data raises **privacy and neutrality** concerns. On balance, the system is a genuine innovation in **service delivery and welfare saturation**, but its long-term value depends on **integrating it under elected panchayats/municipalities**, ensuring political neutrality, and pairing administrative reach with genuine **devolution of the 3 Fs** to local bodies.
keyPoints: Launched 2 Oct 2019; ~15,004 Grama and 3,842 Ward Sachivalayams for doorstep service delivery.
Volunteers (each ~50 households) enable last-mile, leakage-reduced DBT welfare delivery.
Benefits: single-window services, addresses functionary deficit, welfare saturation.
Limitation: administrative layer must not overshadow the constitutional Gram Sabha/elected panchayat.
Concerns: fiscal sustainability, data privacy and political neutrality of Volunteers.
Way forward: integrate under elected local bodies and pair with genuine 3-Fs devolution.
items.source: Government of Andhra Pradesh — Grama/Ward Sachivalayam programme (launched 2 October 2019)
